articles.title: Warning issued after damaged footbridge discovered near Paper House in Norden
articles.excerpt: A snapped wooden plank has left part of the footbridge near the Paper House in Norden damaged, with walkers being urged to take extra care and consider alternative routes until repairs are carried out.
articles.content_html:
Walkers are being urged to take extra care after part of the footbridge near the Paper House in Norden was found to have been damaged.

A wooden plank on the bridge has snapped in half, creating a potential trip hazard for anyone crossing, particularly during busy periods or in poor light. Residents using the route are being advised to slow down, watch their footing and take extra care until repairs can be carried out.

The bridge forms part of a popular walking route used by local residents, dog walkers and visitors exploring the countryside around Norden. With the area attracting large numbers of people during the summer months, the damage could present a risk if left unattended.

Anyone with young children, pushchairs or limited mobility may wish to consider using an alternative route where possible until the bridge has been repaired. Nearby public footpaths and road crossings provide alternative access around the area, although some routes may take slightly longer.

Residents are encouraged to report the damage to the relevant authority if it has not already been logged, helping ensure repairs can be scheduled as quickly as possible.

Until then, anyone planning to use the bridge is asked to remain vigilant, take care when crossing and look out for other walkers who may not have seen the damaged section.

articles.title: Why are so many taxis in Heywood licensed in Wolverhampton and other areas?
articles.excerpt: Many private hire vehicles working in Heywood display licence plates issued by Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other distant councils. Here is why the practice is legal, why it remains controversial and when an offence may be committed.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have increasingly been asking the same question: why are so many taxis driving around the town registered in Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other places?

For many people, the sight of private hire vehicles displaying licences issued by councils hundreds of miles away raises concerns about who regulates them, whether they are operating legally and who is responsible if something goes wrong.

The issue has become controversial across England, with local authorities, taxi trade representatives and residents questioning whether the current licensing system gives councils enough control over the vehicles regularly working in their communities.

Why is it controversial?

The debate centres on cross-border licensing.

Since changes introduced under the Deregulation Act 2015, private hire vehicles are no longer expected to work primarily within the area that licensed them. As a result, a driver licensed by Wolverhampton City Council can legally spend most of the working day carrying passengers in Greater Manchester, provided the vehicle and driver comply with the law governing private hire bookings.

Critics argue that the system has weakened local oversight. Drivers may work almost exclusively in Greater Manchester despite being licensed by an authority many miles away, while local councils have less direct control over drivers they did not licence themselves.

Residents may also be unsure which authority they should contact if they wish to make a complaint. Enforcement can become more complicated when several licensing authorities are involved, while different councils may apply different licensing policies and standards.

These concerns have been raised by local authorities across England for several years, with many calling on the Government to reform private hire legislation and give councils greater control over vehicles operating regularly within their boundaries.

Does that mean these vehicles are operating illegally?

No. Although the system is controversial, simply seeing a vehicle licensed in Wolverhampton, Knowsley or another authority driving around Heywood does not mean it is breaking the law.

Private hire licensing works differently from the licensing of traditional taxis.

Unlike a hackney carriage, which can be hailed in the street or wait on an official taxi rank, a private hire vehicle must be pre-booked through a licensed private hire operator before the journey begins.

A Wolverhampton-licensed vehicle seen driving through Heywood could lawfully be travelling to collect a passenger who has already booked, dropping off a customer, waiting for its next booking through an operator or app, or returning from a previous fare.

The licence plate alone does not indicate whether the vehicle is acting lawfully.

When would it become an offence?

The law is much clearer if a private hire vehicle accepts work without a booking.

A private hire driver cannot legally accept passengers who flag the vehicle down in the street, wait on designated taxi ranks or carry passengers without a booking that has first been accepted by a licensed private hire operator.

Those activities are generally reserved for licensed hackney carriage taxis.

If residents witness a private hire vehicle picking up passengers without a booking, licensing officers can investigate whether an offence has been committed.

Who is responsible for enforcement?

One reason the issue generates debate is that responsibility can involve several organisations.

The council that issued the driver's licence retains important regulatory powers and can investigate complaints or suspend and revoke licences where appropriate.

Greater Manchester Police can deal with suspected criminal offences, while local licensing officers may carry out roadside inspections and joint enforcement operations with other authorities.

Many licensing authorities now share intelligence and work together to improve enforcement across council boundaries.

Why Wolverhampton?

Wolverhampton has become one of the country's largest private hire licensing authorities.

Over recent years it has processed applications from drivers across England, meaning many vehicles operating in towns and cities far from the West Midlands legitimately display Wolverhampton licence plates.

The same principle applies to vehicles licensed by authorities such as Knowsley and other councils outside Greater Manchester.

The bigger debate

The growing number of vehicles displaying out-of-area licences has become a national political issue.

Supporters of the current system argue that it provides flexibility for drivers, supports competition and allows passengers to access transport more easily, particularly through app-based booking services.

Critics believe councils should have greater powers over vehicles that spend most of their time working within their communities, regardless of where those vehicles and drivers were originally licensed.

Successive governments have considered reforms to taxi and private hire legislation, but cross-border private hire work remains lawful under the current framework.

What should residents know?

For anyone wondering why so many vehicles in Heywood display Wolverhampton, Knowsley or other out-of-area licence plates, the answer is that the law allows it.

Their presence alone is not evidence of illegal activity.

The important legal question is not where the vehicle is licensed, but whether it is operating as a genuine private hire vehicle, with every journey properly pre-booked through a licensed operator.

Where there is evidence that a private hire vehicle is accepting passengers without bookings or otherwise breaking licensing rules, those concerns can be investigated by the relevant licensing authority and, where appropriate, the police.

articles.title: Concerns Raised Over Grooming Gangs and Child Exploitation in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The issue of grooming gangs and child sexual exploitation continues to pose significant challenges in the UK, with Rochdale highlighted in ongoing investigations.
articles.content_html:
The issue of grooming gangs and child sexual exploitation has remained one of the most serious social challenges facing the United Kingdom. Over the past two decades, investigations have revealed troubling patterns in various towns, including Rochdale.

Authorities have faced scrutiny regarding their handling of these cases, with calls for improved measures to protect vulnerable individuals. The impact of these issues extends beyond immediate victims, affecting families and communities.

Rochdale has been notably mentioned in discussions surrounding these investigations, prompting local leaders to address the ongoing concerns. The community remains vigilant as efforts to tackle these issues continue.

As investigations progress, the focus remains on ensuring the safety and well-being of children and young people, with a commitment to preventing future exploitation.

articles.title: Bill Oddie Reflects on Rochdale Roots in BBC Documentary
articles.excerpt: Bill Oddie, the star of The Goodies and Springwatch, explored his Rochdale heritage in a recent episode of Who Do You Think You Are?, revealing family history and personal insights.
articles.content_html:
Bill Oddie, the renowned television personality known for his work on The Goodies and Springwatch, recently revisited his Rochdale roots in an episode of the BBC series Who Do You Think You Are?. Born in 1941 at Birch Hill Hospital in Littleborough, Oddie moved away from Rochdale at the age of seven when his father secured a job in Birmingham.

During the documentary, Oddie discovered that his ancestors were predominantly mill workers. He learned that his grandmother, Emily Worrall, who played a significant role in his upbringing, was born in Rochdale and likely worked at Arrow Mill in Castleton from the age of 13. Oddie reflected on his complicated relationship with his father, attributing it to his grandmother's influence, while also acknowledging her impact on his passion for birds.

The programme also shed light on Oddie's mother, Lilian, who was committed to a psychiatric institution during his childhood. He had long believed she suffered from schizophrenia and had abandoned him, but he later learned from nurses that she was actually a manic depressive. Oddie's mother had experienced significant trauma, including the loss of a daughter shortly before his birth, which he had not fully understood until now.

Oddie expressed that this journey into his family's past has been transformative, allowing him to reassess his feelings towards his mother. He stated, "This journey has been a real lifesaver... I wish I'd known her better and I wish she'd known me." His reflections highlight the complexities of familial relationships and the impact of understanding one's history.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Faces £15m Budget Deficit by 2029
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council is projected to face a £15m budget deficit by 2029 if no action is taken, according to the latest financial forecast presented at a town hall meeting.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is facing a projected budget deficit of £15.227 million by the financial year 2029/30 if no action is taken. The latest budget forecast, presented at a town hall meeting, highlights that this shortfall is anticipated due to wage increases, inflation, and rising costs in adult social care and children’s services.

The finance team has expressed uncertainty regarding the annual government funding settlement, which is expected to contribute to the financial challenges. Budget documents indicate a risk that the finance settlement for 2029/30 may not include a continuation of the Recovery Grant, which is currently confirmed only until 2028/29 and amounts to approximately £15 million.

In adult social care, the 'real living wage' is increasing beyond expected levels, further straining budgets. An additional allocation of £1.5 million per year has been factored into future costs. Overspending in children’s services has also exceeded initial forecasts, a trend noted in recent years. Finance boss Sam Smith reported that inflation on wages for council staff is compounding these budget pressures.

During the meeting on July 28, Councillor Daniel Meredith stated that significant efforts are underway to develop new care homes and children’s homes, expressing optimism about addressing the challenges in both adult and children’s services. The council has made savings of £204.5 million from its revenue budget since 2010/11, but the projected gaps indicate that savings of £6 million will be required by 2028/29, escalating to £15 million by 2029/30.

articles.title: Rochdale Local Plan Advances Towards Public Consultation
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Local Plan, which outlines development and housing strategies until 2039, is set for public consultation following approval from council leaders.
articles.content_html:
A plan that will shape Rochdale's future over the next 13 years has moved closer to implementation after receiving approval from council leaders. The Rochdale Local Plan outlines how the borough will develop, including the construction of nearly 11,000 new homes and significant changes to local transport stations.

The council has refined a 175-page document, which will now undergo public consultation. The formal adoption of the plan is expected later in 2027. Initially, the plan required new housing developments to include 20 per cent affordable housing, but this threshold has been adjusted to 15 per cent due to financial viability concerns. Councillor Daniel Meredith stated that this change does not reflect a reduced commitment to affordable housing, noting that the council has delivered 883 affordable homes in the past five years, exceeding the previous target.

Housing is a major focus of the Local Plan, with designated land for new homes already identified in the Places for Everyone strategy. This broader plan aims to deliver around 175,000 homes across Greater Manchester over the next two decades and is anticipated to attract investment and redevelopment in Rochdale.

The Local Plan also includes the Rochdale Rail Corridor Strategy, which aims to enhance transport hubs along the Manchester to Leeds railway line. This initiative seeks to create vibrant areas for living, working, and recreation around stations in Rochdale and nearby locations, supported by improved walking and cycling routes and community spaces. The strategic plan addresses various topics, including climate, economic growth, and sustainable transport, influencing the borough's growth trajectory.

articles.title: Severely Neglected Toddler Rushed to Hospital After Social Services Case Closed
articles.excerpt: A 19-month-old girl, referred to as Child K1, was admitted to hospital in critical condition after social services closed her case, revealing severe neglect and malnutrition.
articles.content_html:
A 19-month-old girl, referred to as Child K1, was admitted to hospital in critical condition 19 days after social services closed her case, according to a Child Safeguarding Practice Review (CSPR) in Rochdale. The report revealed that the toddler was severely neglected, weighing just 9.7lb (4.4kg) at the time of her admission, which is less than half the average weight for her age.

The review, conducted by expert reviewer Nicki Walker-Hall, found that the child was suffering from severe dehydration and had no fatty tissue on her body. She was described as having "paper-thin skin" and was covered in open pressure sores extending along her back, hips and bottom. The case was closed despite previous warnings about a mother, who was just 17 when the child was born, neglecting her daughter.

Concerns about Child K1's welfare were raised multiple times before her hospital admission. A family member had informed hospital staff in April 2024 that the mother was neglecting the child, but social services concluded that the mother was willing to accept support. However, subsequent visits revealed that the basic needs of the child were not being met, and the mother avoided contact with social workers and health visitors.

Following an anonymous tip in December 2024, social workers visited the home and confirmed the child's condition. Despite this, they were unable to secure the mother's consent for further intervention, leading to the case being closed. The review concluded that the child's severe malnutrition and dehydration could have led to death if emergency treatment had not been administered in time.

articles.title: Rochdale Veteran Seeks Justice Following Nuclear Tests
articles.excerpt: John Morris, a Rochdale veteran exposed to nuclear tests in the 1950s, expresses renewed hope for justice following the appointment of Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who supports an independent inquiry.
articles.content_html:
A man from Rochdale who was exposed to nuclear tests in the 1950s has expressed renewed hope for justice following the appointment of Prime Minister Andy Burnham. John Morris, now 88, was sent to Christmas Island in the Pacific Ocean at the age of 18, where he witnessed a series of nuclear detonations conducted by the Ministry of Defence (MoD).

Morris is part of a group of veterans who have lodged a criminal complaint against the MoD, claiming they have been denied justice regarding the health issues they suffered as a result of the tests. Many veterans have reported serious medical problems and are calling for an independent inquiry into their treatment. Burnham has previously supported the veterans' cause, stating that there is clear evidence of misconduct in public office. He has indicated that he backs a judicial review into the matter, which has given Morris and others hope for a resolution after years of campaigning.

The MoD has stated that compensation is available through the War Pensions Scheme, but many veterans feel this is insufficient. Morris believes that with Burnham's support, there is a chance for a thorough investigation into their claims. He has said that the new Prime Minister has finally given him hope of getting justice, as he continues to advocate for the rights of veterans affected by the nuclear tests.

In 2025, when Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester, he expressed his view that the investigation into the treatment of veterans could not wait any longer, especially following the 80th anniversary of VE Day. Morris and his fellow veterans are now looking to the new Prime Minister to take decisive action on their behalf.
